overview.title: Simple hold-out validation and the start of K-fold validation
overview.main_topic: The simple hold-out validation protocol (Figure 5.12, Listing 5.5), its weakness on small datasets, and the opening definition of K-fold validation
overview.central_idea: Hold-out validation sets aside a fixed slice of the data for validation, tunes the model against it, then retrains the final model on all non-test data and evaluates once on the test set. It is simple but unreliable when data is scarce, because a small validation set gives scores that swing with the random split; K-fold validation is introduced as the remedy.
overview.importance: This is the first of the three evaluation protocols the book recommends (it summarizes them again on p.205). Choosing a protocol is a mandatory step of every project in the universal workflow of chapter 6, and the 'retrain on all non-test data' pattern in Listing 5.5 is standard practice.
learning_objectives: Describe the hold-out validation protocol and draw its data split
Read Listing 5.5 line by line and explain the role of each step, including the final retraining on training + validation data
Explain why the test set must not be used for tuning, and why a validation set is therefore needed in addition
Recognize the symptom that indicates a validation set is too small (scores vary strongly between random shuffles)
State the basic K-fold procedure: K equal partitions, train on K-1, evaluate on the remaining one
prerequisites: Difference between parameters and hyperparameters, and the notion of information leaks (p.173)
The validation sets set aside in chapter 4 (p.135, p.144) and K-fold validation on the housing data (p.153)

summary:
The page finishes the sentence from p.173 announcing that the chapter will later discuss **common-sense baselines** (section 5.2.2, p.176), then presents the first concrete evaluation protocol.

**Simple hold-out validation.** You set apart part of the data as a test set and train on the rest. Because tuning the model on the test set would leak information about it into the model (the argument made on p.173), you *also* reserve a validation set. Figure 5.12 shows the split: of the "total available labeled data", the large left block is the **training set** ("train on this"), and a smaller right block is the **held-out validation set** ("evaluate on this").

**Listing 5.5** implements it with labels omitted: it shuffles `data`, takes the first `num_validation_samples = 10000` samples as `validation_data` and the rest as `training_data`, builds a model with `get_model()`, fits on the training data and computes `validation_score`. The `...` stands for the tuning loop: tune, retrain, re-evaluate, repeat. Once the hyperparameters are fixed, the callout notes it is common to **train the final model from scratch on all non-test data** (`np.concatenate([training_data, validation_data])`) and only then compute `test_score` on `test_data`.

**The flaw.** With little data, the validation and test sets may be too small to be statistically representative. The diagnostic is simple: if different random shuffles before splitting give very different performance measures, you have this problem. **K-fold validation** and **iterated K-fold validation** address it.

**K-fold validation** begins at the bottom: split the data into `K` equal partitions; for each partition `i`, train a model on the other `K - 1` partitions and evaluate it on partition `i`. The averaging of the K scores, Figure 5.13 and Listing 5.6 follow on p.175.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The end of a sentence begun on p.173: after explaining the three evaluation protocols, the authors will discuss common-sense baselines that check whether training is getting anywhere.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Evaluation has two parts: a protocol that gives a trustworthy score, and a reference point that tells you whether the score is any good. This line points ahead to the second part.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A validation score means little on its own; 70% accuracy is good on a 10-class problem and poor on a binary problem where one class makes up 90% of the data.

terminology.meaning: The score of a trivial non-learning strategy (random guessing, always predicting the majority class, etc.) that a model must beat to be useful.

paragraphs.excerpt: Set apart some fraction of your data as your test set. Train
paragraphs.what_it_says: Hold-out validation: reserve part of the data as a test set and train on the rest. Since you must not tune the model on the test set (to avoid information leaks), you also reserve a separate validation set.
paragraphs.what_it_means: There are really two hold-outs. The test set is touched once at the end; the validation set is used over and over during development as the feedback signal for hyperparameter choices. The word *also* (italic in the book) stresses that the validation set is in addition to the test set, not a replacement for it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Every hyperparameter choice made by looking at a score leaks a little information about the data that produced the score. Keeping the test set untouched keeps its estimate of generalization unbiased.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Partition the labeled data D into disjoint sets D_train, D_val, D_test. Parameters are fit on D_train, hyperparameters are chosen on D_val, and generalization is estimated once on D_test.

terminology.meaning: Data kept out of training and used only for evaluation.
Information about the evaluation data reaching the model through your tuning decisions, even though the model never trains on that data directly (p.173).

connections: p.173: The argument for three sets and the definition of information leaks.

paragraphs.excerpt: This is the simplest evaluation protocol, and it suffers from one flaw:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Hold-out validation is the simplest protocol but has one flaw: with little data, validation and test sets may be too small to be statistically representative. You can tell because different random shuffles before splitting give very different performance measures. K-fold and iterated K-fold validation fix this.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A score measured on a small set is a noisy estimate. If you get 85% with one shuffle and 78% with another, the split, not the model, is driving the number, so you cannot use it to compare hyperparameter settings reliably.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Model selection is only as good as the signal it uses. On small datasets (like the 404-sample Boston housing training set in chapter 4) a single hold-out split can lead you to the wrong configuration.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: for accuracy measured on n validation samples, the standard error is about sqrt(p(1-p)/n). With p = 0.8 and n = 100 that is 0.04 (4 points); with n = 10,000 it is 0.004. Small n makes run-to-run swings large.

terminology.meaning: Large and varied enough that statistics computed on it (like accuracy) are close to those on the whole data distribution.
How much the measured score changes when the random split changes.

connections: p.153: The housing example used K-fold validation because a ~100-sample validation set would have high variance.
p.176: Iterated K-fold validation with shuffling is described there.

paragraphs.what_it_says: K-fold validation: split data into K equal partitions. For each partition i, train a model on the other K - 1 partitions and evaluate on partition i.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Every sample is used for validation exactly once and for training K - 1 times. K models are trained, one per fold; their scores are averaged (stated on p.175).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Averaging over K different validation sets reduces the dependence of the estimate on one lucky or unlucky split, at the cost of K times the training compute.
paragraphs.technical_idea: With N samples, each fold has N/K samples; each model trains on N(K-1)/K samples.

terminology.meaning: One of the K equal-size disjoint subsets of the data.

concepts.name: Simple hold-out validation
concepts.definition: An evaluation protocol that sets aside a fixed fraction of the non-test data as a validation set, trains on the rest, and uses the validation score to tune hyperparameters.
concepts.intuition: Keep a sealed exam for the end (test set) and a practice exam you can look at as often as you like (validation set).
concepts.technical: One random split; one model per configuration. The final model is usually retrained on training + validation data after tuning, then evaluated once on the test set (Listing 5.5).
concepts.significance: The default protocol when data is plentiful (p.205: 'In most cases, the first will work well enough').
concepts.example: Listing 5.5 holds out 10,000 samples for validation.
concepts.misconception: That the validation score is an unbiased estimate of real-world performance. After many tuning rounds it is optimistically biased; that is why the test set exists.

concepts.name: Validation set
concepts.definition: Data held out from training and used as the feedback signal for tuning hyperparameters.
concepts.intuition: The practice exam that guides your study choices.
concepts.technical: Separate from both training data (used to fit weights) and test data (used once for the final estimate).
concepts.significance: Prevents tuning on the test set, which would leak information and inflate the reported score.
concepts.misconception: That because the model never trains on validation data, it cannot overfit to it. Tuning based on validation scores is itself a form of learning (p.173).

concepts.name: Information leak
concepts.definition: Information about evaluation data reaching the model through the developer's decisions.
concepts.intuition: Each time you peek at the exam score and adjust, you learn a little about the exam itself.
concepts.technical: Choosing hyperparameters by maximizing a score on a fixed set selects for configurations that happen to do well on that particular set.
concepts.significance: The reason a test set must stay untouched until the end.
concepts.example: Trying 100 learning rates and reporting the best validation score gives an optimistic estimate.
concepts.misconception: That leaks only happen when evaluation samples are in the training data.

concepts.name: K-fold validation
concepts.definition: Split data into K equal partitions; for each partition, train on the other K - 1 and evaluate on it; average the K scores.
concepts.intuition: Rotate which slice of the data plays the role of the practice exam, so no single split decides the result.
concepts.technical: K models are trained; each sample is validated on exactly once. The averaging step is stated on p.175.
concepts.significance: Gives a lower-variance performance estimate when data is scarce.
concepts.example: With K = 3 and 300 samples, three models each train on 200 and validate on 100.
concepts.misconception: That K-fold removes the need for a test set; p.175 notes it does not exempt you from a distinct validation set for calibration, and a final test set is still needed.

math.title: Fold sizes in K-fold validation
math.source_text: split your data into K partitions of equal size. For each partition i, train a model on the remaining K - 1 partitions

variables.meaning: Partition i, used for validation in run i
The remaining K - 1 partitions, used for training in run i

math.operations: Division of the dataset into equal parts; set difference.
math.purpose: Quantifies how much data each of the K models sees for training and validation.
math.interpretation: Larger K means each model trains on more data (closer to the full set) but costs more models.
math.intuition: Every sample sits in exactly one validation fold.
math.numerical_example: N = 400, K = 4: each fold has 100 samples; each model trains on 300 and validates on 100; 4 models are trained.

code.title: Hold-out validation (note that labels are omitted for simplicity)
code.original_code:
num_validation_samples = 10000
np.random.shuffle(data)
validation_data = data[:num_validation_samples]
training_data = data[num_validation_samples:]
model = get_model()
model.fit(training_data, ...)
validation_score = model.evaluate(validation_data, ...)
...
model = get_model()
model.fit(
    np.concatenate([training_data, validation_data]),
    ...,
)
test_score = model.evaluate(test_data, ...)
code.what_it_does: Schematic code for the hold-out protocol: shuffle, split off a validation set, train and validate, tune (elided), then retrain a fresh model on all non-test data and compute the test score.

line_explanations.explanation: Size of the validation set: 10,000 samples.
Shuffle the data in place; the callout says shuffling is usually appropriate (p.177 explains when it is not: time-ordered data).
First 10,000 samples become the validation set (callout: 'Defines the validation set').
The remaining samples become the training set (callout: 'Defines the training set').
Build a fresh model, train it on the training data and evaluate on the validation data.
The `...` is the tuning loop: 'At this point, you can tune your model, retrain it, evaluate it, tune it again, and so on.'
With hyperparameters fixed, build a new model from scratch and train it on training + validation data concatenated, i.e. all non-test data.
Evaluate once on the untouched test set.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: an array `data` (labels omitted), a separate `test_data`, and a model-building function `get_model()`. Outputs: `validation_score` (used for tuning) and `test_score` (final estimate).
code.algorithm: shuffle -> split -> fit/evaluate -> tune loop -> refit on train+val -> test once
code.theory_link: Implements the three-set discipline of p.173: validation data is the feedback signal, test data is used only once.

parameters.name: num_validation_samples
parameters.role: Size of the held-out validation set.

parameters.name: get_model()
parameters.role: Placeholder function returning a freshly compiled, untrained model with the chosen hyperparameters.

pitfalls: `np.random.shuffle(data)` shuffles only `data`; with real labels you must shuffle inputs and labels with the same permutation.
Shuffling is wrong for time series (temporal leak, p.177).
When refitting on train+val, settings tuned on the training size (e.g. number of epochs) may need slight adjustment because there is more data.
Calling `get_model()` again is essential: reusing the trained model would continue training instead of starting from scratch.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: same protocol with labels kept aligned
import numpy as np
idx = np.random.permutation(len(x))
x, y = x[idx], y[idx]
n_val = 10000
x_val, y_val = x[:n_val], y[:n_val]
x_tr, y_tr = x[n_val:], y[n_val:]
model = get_model()
model.fit(x_tr, y_tr, epochs=20, validation_data=(x_val, y_val))
# ... tune ...
model = get_model()
model.fit(np.concatenate([x_tr, x_val]), np.concatenate([y_tr, y_val]), epochs=20)
test_score = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)

deeper.title: Why retrain on training + validation data at the end?
deeper.body: The callout says it is *common* to train the final model from scratch on all non-test data. Beyond the book: the reasons are (1) more training data usually improves generalization, and the validation data has already done its job of selecting hyperparameters; (2) the test score then measures exactly the model you will deploy. The cost is that you have no validation set left to monitor this final run, so choices like the number of epochs must be fixed in advance from the tuning phase.

deeper.title: How small is 'too small'? A numerical look
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: treat each validation prediction as a coin flip that is correct with probability $p$. The measured accuracy on $n$ samples has standard deviation $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

| n | std. dev. at p = 0.8 |
|---|---|
| 100 | 4.0 points |
| 1,000 | 1.3 points |
| 10,000 | 0.4 points |

With 100 validation samples, two configurations that differ by 3 points are indistinguishable from noise, which is exactly the symptom the book describes (very different scores across shuffles).

deeper.title: Practice exams and the final exam
deeper.body: A student who studies by repeatedly taking the same practice exam and adjusting their study plan will eventually ace that practice exam without necessarily mastering the subject. The final exam, never seen before, is what reveals true understanding. The validation set is the practice exam; the test set is the final.

misconceptions.claim: Two sets (train and test) are enough if I never train on the test set.
misconceptions.correction: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set leaks information into the model; you need a separate validation set for tuning (p.173-174).

misconceptions.claim: The final model should be the one trained during tuning, on training data only.
misconceptions.correction: The book notes it is common to retrain from scratch on all non-test data (training + validation) once hyperparameters are fixed.

misconceptions.claim: If my validation score is stable from epoch to epoch, my validation set is big enough.
misconceptions.correction: The book's diagnostic is across different random shuffles/splits of the data, not across epochs.

takeaways: Hold-out validation: test set reserved, then a fixed validation slice of the remaining data guides tuning.
Never tune on the test set; reserve a validation set as well.
After tuning, it is common to retrain from scratch on training + validation data and evaluate once on test.
Its flaw: small validation/test sets give noisy, unrepresentative scores; diagnose by re-splitting with different shuffles.
K-fold validation trains on K - 1 partitions and evaluates on the remaining one, rotating through all K.

questions.question: In Listing 5.5, what data is the final model trained on before computing test_score?
questions.explanation: The listing calls model.fit(np.concatenate([training_data, validation_data]), ...): all non-test data. Training only on training_data is what happens during tuning; using validation alone would waste data; including test_data would leak the test set.

questions.question: What symptom tells you that your hold-out validation set is too small?
questions.answer: Different random shuffles of the data before splitting give very different measures of model performance.
questions.explanation: This is the diagnostic stated on the page: high variance of the score across splits means the validation set is not statistically representative.

questions.question: Why does hold-out validation need a validation set in addition to the test set, even though the model is never trained on the test set?
questions.answer: Because tuning hyperparameters based on test performance leaks information about the test set into the model, making the test score optimistically biased. The validation set absorbs that tuning so the test set stays an unbiased final check.
questions.explanation: The page says 'to prevent information leaks, you shouldn't tune your model based on the test set', referring back to the argument on p.173 that tuning is itself a form of learning.

questions.question: You have 600 non-test samples and use K = 3 fold validation. How many samples does each model train on and validate on, and how many models are trained?
questions.answer: Each fold has 200 samples; each model trains on 400 and validates on 200; 3 models are trained.
questions.explanation: Partitions of equal size N/K = 200; training uses the remaining K - 1 = 2 partitions.

questions.question: Why does Listing 5.5 call get_model() a second time before the final fit?
options: To start training from scratch rather than continuing from the tuned weights
questions.answer: To start training from scratch rather than continuing from the tuned weights
questions.explanation: The callout says to 'train your final model from scratch on all non-test data'. The architecture is unchanged (same tuned hyperparameters); evaluate() does not delete models; get_model() has nothing to do with data loading.

questions.question: Listing 5.5 shuffles before splitting. Name a situation where this would be a mistake.
questions.answer: When predicting the future from the past (time series): shuffling creates a temporal leak, so the test data should be strictly later than the training data.
questions.explanation: The callout says shuffling is 'usually' appropriate; p.177 explains the arrow-of-time exception.
